elements.text: Food reached your stomach, air reached your lungs — but who delivers them to every single cell?
Every cell needs oxygen and glucose — 24x7
One pump — about 100,000 beats every day
Top two = atria (they RECEIVE blood). Bottom two = ventricles (they PUMP it out).
Blood passes through the heart TWICE in one full round — that's why it's called 'double circulation'
O2 from the lungs → heart → body → CO2 back → lungs. And in the middle: the pump.

beats.narration: Today we're going to meet the hardest-working organ in your body. It never takes a day off — it's working even while you sleep. Let's begin.

beats.topic: Why we need a delivery system
beats.narration: Let's start with a question. Food has reached your stomach, and oxygen has reached your lungs. But the cells in your little toe need both. So who carries them all the way there? That is exactly what circulation does.

The engine of this system is the heart. Don't think of it as something magical — it is simply a pump. Made of muscle, about the size of your fist, and it beats close to one hundred thousand times a day.

beats.topic: Four chambers — RA, LA, RV, LV
beats.narration: Now look inside the pump. There are four rooms. The top two are the atria — they receive blood. The bottom two are the ventricles — they push blood out. The right side and the left side do different jobs, and that difference is the whole story ahead.

The first loop is short. The right ventricle sends blood full of carbon dioxide to the lungs. There, the blood drops off CO2, picks up fresh oxygen, and returns to the left atrium. This loop is called pulmonary circulation.

The second loop is the long one. The left ventricle — the strongest chamber of all — pushes oxygen-rich blood to the entire body, from your head to your toes. The cells take the oxygen, hand back carbon dioxide, and the blood returns to the right atrium.

Now watch carefully — to complete one full round, the blood passed through the heart twice. Once on its way to the lungs, and once on its way to the body. That is why we call it double circulation. Exams love asking this directly.

So here is the whole story in one line: oxygen from the lungs, a push from the heart, delivery to the body, carbon dioxide back, and around again. If anything felt unclear, just raise your hand — I'm right here.
